utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Please call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, thank you, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I just want to check whether the translation into is -- This Thursday, 27th September. I welcome the representatives of the Prosecution. I also welcome Mr. Seselj and all the persons who are present in this courtroom. So today we have all morning. We have four hours, during which I will tell you about a certain number of questions, and Mr. Seselj and Ms. Dahl may intervene if they have also some concerns or topics which they wish to talk about. First of all, there is the delicate, Mr. Seselj, which concerns you directly. Principally, you will have noted, and I will be very candid with you, that there is a procedure which has been put in place for the hearings, which is the following: I am the first one to enter, and then you come in the room second. Why? The reason why is to avoid a problem, the problem which you had talked about when you don't rise when the Judge or the Judges enter the courtroom. Therefore, I have given a 50 per cent solution to the problem. There is anther a 50 per cent problem which I did not solve, because when I leave, or when the members of the Chamber leave the courtroom, you are not going to rise. Therefore, I have pondered about the reasons which are your -- which motivate your attitude. I suppose you are doing this because you said that you contest the existence of the Tribunal, and, therefore, it is your way of showing that you are opposed to the Tribunal. So this, of course, is your choice. And I may understand your position myself, but I'm not alone. Why am I not alone? Well, because, we are in a court which follows certain rituals, ceremonials, and there are also people in the public gallery as you know it. It's also broadcast and put on the internet. There are some people who are watching. There will be witnesses who will come who may have been victims in certain cases or because of certain facts; and for these victims, for these persons, for the people who are watching and all persons who are watching, the fact of not rising might be interpreted by these people as a refusal of everything, as being discourteous or as a behaviour, which would be a form of contempt, of course. For the moment I am alone, sitting alone. Soon, I will have two other colleagues for the trial itself. I do not know what my colleagues will think. As far as I'm concerned, I do not wish your attitude to be in any way prejudicial to you. As I told you, to my mind, you are presumed innocent. Therefore, you are a person, a citizen, a human person worthy of respect, my respect, with rights, and who therefore within this court will have a role to play in the coming weeks. If you remain seated, in order to show your opposition or disapproval of the Tribunal and to the person of the Judges themselves, I don't know, maybe the way it is perceived by the Judges themselves or others may be negative. So this is what I wanted to tell you first. For the moment, I try and avoid the problem, but I can only avoid 50 per cent of the consequences, and I will not be able to avoid the problem when there will be a witness and when the Chamber will be complete; and, then, the usher will ask everybody to rise, all rise, and you will not rise. You will remain seated. So this will be seen. It will be commented in the press, and the witness will also notice. This is the problem, and you certainly have your own reasons. Perhaps you could let me know. You now have the floor, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, you are quite right on one issue. I really do not recognise and never will recognise the legality and legitimacy of this Tribunal. I told you this several months ago. That is my right. However, I do admit that this Tribunal is a material force which is capable of imprisoning me, holding me here illegally for five years, and organising for to me put up trial. That's my starting point. I, therefore, felt it was better and more in my interests for me to respond to the summons by this illegal court and to oppose the illegal charges against me, the false charges against me here. That's why I have decided to participate in this process. Secondly, in the Serbian legal system, this custom does not exist. Nobody rises when a Judge enters the courtroom. Nobody rises when a Chamber leaves the courtroom. There's only one instance when people rise and that's when the judgement is being handed down, but then everybody stands up, including the Judges and everybody else present, not just the accused. This is not the practice here, but I am adhering to the Serbian legal system, and I will not desist from this. Thirdly, there is no rule, no regulation, law or by law binding anyone to conduct or engage in any kind of gymnastics or to rise when a Chamber comes in and goes out. This is just a custom that nobody has opposed. You know what the laws here are like. All they care about is keeping their good salaries. So nobody has raised this issue apart from me. Something happened when I was a witness in the case against Mr. Milosevic. For three or four days, as a witness, I did not wish to rise, and then Judge Robinson threatened that he might interrupt my testimony. Under threat of having my testimony interrupted, and I cared a lot about testifying, I said, "I agree. I will rise here, but I will never rise in my own case." This may represent a problem to you and your colleagues, and you have to solve it. How you will solve me if I will not submit to your will, how can you solve it? You can impose sanctions; for example, you can characterise my behaviour as an aggravating circumstance. You can increase my sentence by 10 years and that will be quite in order. I will understand it, but I will not rise because I have no reason to rise for anyone. I can rise or kneel only before God; but to another human being, no. Of course, there are certain conventions governing this custom, when one rises, in order to show one's respect to a friend or somebody else. But to throw somebody under your feet just because he has been falsely accused, that is something I will not stand for. I will not bear it. It is your prerogative to impose a sanction on me, and I will accept it. Determine a certain number of years of imprisonment more and everything will be all right. In this case, you know, there's another point to be raised. By your leave, just let me say this. When I first appeared before this Court, I raised the issue of the clothes worn by the Judges, the Registry, and the Prosecution. That also is a problem for me. You once attempted to answer that question of mine, but I was not satisfied with your answer. However, I did not have time to express my disagreement because we had more serious things to deal with. You said that, in every court, there are special ways for Judges and other personnel to dress, but this has never existed in the Serbian court. There are no Judges' robes in Serbian courts, no special clothes for the Prosecution, no special clothes for members of the Registry. In Serb courts, everybody's only duty-bound to appear in decent, normal clothes; nothing more than that. I'm adhering to the principles that apply in the Serbian legal system, especially bearing in mind that no regulations or rules exist here regulating that. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence might be changed or the Statute might be changed to introduce this, or the president of the Tribunal can issue binding instructions, but that then will not apply to me but to future trials. It cannot apply to me retroactively. No legal norms that are prejudicial to me can be applied to me retroactively, and such a rule or norm would certainly be prejudicial to me because it would force me to engage in gymnastics in the courtroom, which I do not wish to engage in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had already explained this, talking about the robes or gowns of the Judges, and your main argument is that, in Serbian law, the Judges do not have gowns, and that, in the courtroom, nobody rises when the Judges enter the courtroom or when they leave the courtroom. Therefore, you consider that there is no reason to act any differently, all the more so as in the Rules it has not been provided for. This is your argument. As for myself, the important point was to understand your position. You have now explained it. I am not going to comment upon it, and I needed to let you know. Last point about the gowns of the Judges. This Tribunal uses them. It could have been in plain clothes. Colours may have been different. I am not the one who decided about this, these rules, and I just apply these regulations, follow them. So that's what I have to say on this specific point. Now we are going to pass to other topics such as the opening date of the trial. First of all, I have to give you some information which are the following: It is agreed that there will be a pre-trial Status Conference on Tuesday, 6 November. If I'm not mistaken, it will be Tuesday, 6 November. I think the legal officer can check. Yes. And at this Status Conference, there will be the two Judges constituting the Bench; and, during this conference for the opening of the trial, this Pre-Trial Conference will be a hearing during which the members of the Chamber will be in a position to determine officially how many hours will be given to the Prosecution and also how many witnesses will come to testify. Also, this conference may be the place and the moment where there will be some debate on residual matters which will not have been completely settled beforehand. So this would be on that Tuesday. On the Wednesday, next day, Ms. Dahl, I suppose, unless it is Ms. Carla Del Ponte herself, will express following the Rules the arguments of the Prosecution in its first statement, in its opening statement. So I have provided for four hours for a complete statement. So that will last for four hours. The next day, that is to say, the Thursday, yourself, Mr. Seselj, if you so wish, because the Rules enables you, allows you not to do so, you will then have the floor for the same time, four hours, in order to make your own opening statement and present your own position, state your own position, on the merits of the indictment. So we have, therefore, these three days which have been scheduled. In the meantime, I have also asked the President of the Tribunal to let him know that the order has scheduled these three days, and the Registrar also is notified, because it is the Registrar, according to the Rules, who must see to it that we will have the necessary courtrooms. The problem we have just now is the following: As you know, because I know you're very well-informed, the Tribunal for the moment is running seven trials and we only have three courtrooms. Therefore, one needs from time to time to have one of the Chambers, which normally sit, would not be sitting, so that the seventh trial can also go forward. Up to now, I have had some information from other Chambers according to which they do not wish to free any courtroom because of their schedule for their own hearings, for their own trial. Therefore, the Registrar and the President of the Tribunal, possibly the coordination committee which has foreseen to agree on these matters. As far as I'm concerned, able be quite firm on this matter, one has waited too much for the opening of your trial and we must begin this trial. In order to do so, one must start the procedure which is foreseen in the Rules, which is to be added another problem, which is the courtroom availability. As you know, there are three courtrooms. I know you will have had an opportunity to go to courtroom I, courtroom II, and courtroom III here. We are in courtroom III. So I suppose, I presume that, once the Prosecutor's opening statement and you were answer will have been made, there will be some public attending in the public gallery, and the members of the press want to be present for these opening statements. Therefore, those hearings will be held only -- they're only possible in courtroom I or courtroom III, because in courtroom II there is -- there are only two seats for the public. Therefore, it has to be either here or in courtroom number I. Courtroom number I, as you know as well as I do, was once reserved for the Milosevic trial. Courtrooms I and III are presently used for multiple-accused trials, and number II is usually a courtroom where you can have three accused, but it's a very small courtroom and the attendance of the public is extremely limited. Therefore, for your own trial, one might use courtroom II when there will be some closed hearings. Because you're in closed hearings, there is no attendance, no public, so there would be no problem. But public hearings with witnesses, public witnesses, or witnesses with protection for their voice or their features or their pseudonym, that will be courtroom I or III. Now, for the moment, I have no answer from the Registry on this matter of available courtrooms, but there is also another question. Once these proceedings will have started, we will have the question of hearing the first witnesses. In theory, normally, following on that, one should start next week with the first witnesses, and there Prosecution will also need to know what is on schedule in order to get these witnesses in The Hague and preparing some proofing. So it is for the Registry to let us know as quickly as possible when this will be possible, because if we meet with an impossibility at a given moment because of the other trials and because the other Judges do not want to leave a courtroom, the best solution then would be to begin the first phase of the trial -- well, first of all, the Pre-Trial Conference and the two hearings with the opening statements, then wait a few days, perhaps one or two weeks even, so that we may then have the possibility to have some courtrooms available. Because with seven trials that are ongoing, we will encounter this sort of problem. So some will have to make sacrifices in order to enable the good running of the seven trials and three courtrooms. If it weren't the case, there would be no possibility to actually manage in a serene way those seven trials in question, and perhaps one day eight trials. But I am not talking about the Status Conferences or the decisions made by the Chambers when trials have finished. So there's a series of problems which add up to all this. Now, having seen these administrative or housekeeping matters, this is not, of course, within your province, but I want to be as transparent as possible, and, therefore, I wish to inform you of all these aspects, because a Status Conferences is the proper place to say everything. My policy is to always tell the truth and let it be known where problems may arise. So, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of making an opening statement straight away. I decided to make the Defence opening statement at the beginning of the Defence case, but I would like to ask you to enable me on the 8th of November to make a statement by the accused according to Rule 84 bis. Last time, when the proceedings were scheduled, it was planned allow me to do this; and, as far as I remember, whether the time limit was three hours or two and a half hours, I can't quite remember now, for this statement by the accused. But, anyway, I now ask as the Prosecution is going to have four hours for their opening statement to allow me four hours on the following day for a statement of the accused, and there was a precedent in the Milosevic case. He was given two days to make the statement of the accused, and then two days later he presented an opening statement with respect to Kosovo and Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina subsequently. So a precedent exists, already existed. So that then would be the statement of the accused that I would like to deliver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, there is no problem at all. As far as I'm concerned, there is no problem at all. The equality of arms, one has to be equitable. The Prosecutor will make its opening statement before that, and it's perfectly normal that you should have a day in order to make your own statement. There will be no problem about that, no question. I assure you that you will have your four hours without any problem. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the second question you raised, this is what I would like to say: I think that the problem of courtroom facilities is not as important because we have videotapes on the internet sites of the Tribunal that can be used, but there are very serious problems there and I expect them to become evermore serious in the future. During the last two Status Conferences, the video sites did not transmit the proceedings. The one but last not at all and the last one just partially. Something was broadcast in English but nothing in Serbian. As these problems do not occur and crop up in the other trials, then my conclusion is that somebody intentionally obstructed this for my proceedings. So it would be a good idea if the Registry were to place on the Tribunal's site the entire process, and then that meets the requirements of the public character of the trial and it doesn't matter whether you will be able to fit in two just journalists in the public gallery or 200. But, as an accused, it is in my interest to see that this problem is resolved, to ensure the public character of the trial and that is why I insist upon this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will look into that personally. As you were speaking, I was looking on the internet to see whether images are being broadcast, and it is indeed the case. I will also check to see whether images are also broadcast on the internet. But if ever what you say is true, in other words, that someone is trying to sabotage the broadcast, that would be extremely serious. So I will look into this point. There is no reason why your trial should not, like all others, be broadcast to the world. Now, the other problem is -- or has to do with sound. You seem to suggest that your language was not broadcast; and, therefore, everything that is interpreted into your language or when you speak yourself, you say this is not broadcast. But that's a bit surprising, because technically the -- there should be no problem with the audio sound. But I will also look into that, and I've taken good note of what you've said. You have already raised the issue once, and I had already looked into it myself and noted at the time that there was a broadcast on the internet, but you've just said that the two previous -- for the two previous conferences that was not the case. So I will look into it and find an explanation, because I wouldn't want anyone to try to do such a thing. As I also read the Belgrade press, I discovered, and perhaps you can give me an explanation on this topic, that you had some problems with the broadcast of the trial. You would like the trial to be broadcast on either public or private channels, I don't know, and it would seem that currently an initiative is being taken so that your trial can be broadcast in your country. From my point of view, there should be no problem with regard to broadcasting the images. Everything that goes on in this courtroom can be broadcast on a television station, be it a private or public channel. So from my point of view, there is absolutely no problem. Would you like to say something on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In Serbia, at present, a petition is being signed for the state television, the Public Service of the Television Service of Serbia is what it's called, to televise this process directly, these proceedings directly, and several thousand signatures have been collected thus far. The outcome is uncertain because this doesn't suit, quite obviously, the regime in Serbia today. They don't want to have televised proceedings. They had an unfortunate experience with Slobodan Milosevic, and their expectations were quite contrary to the effect the legal proceedings had in public, but that's a matter of internal Serbian affairs. But there are private television channels which are prepared to televise the proceedings directly, but this would require cooperation from the Registry, which means that the Registry should allow the use of satellite links under the same conditions provided at some -- by the B92 television station, which is a pro-Western television station financed by Soros, the Western Intelligence Services, and so on; in other words, it is anti-Serb television station. Now, they have no idea and no intention of doing that. I would like the patriotic private television channel, who would like to organise televised broadcasting, be allowed to have the same conditions as the B92 television station did formerly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. While you were speaking, I was looking into it. I would like this to be reflected in the transcript. As you were speaking, I noted on the screen that all we see in terms of broadcasting of trials are images of courtrooms I, II, and III, but, in fact, there was no image, and just a few seconds ago it appeared. So is there a relation of cause and effect that suddenly the images have appeared? Currently, all three courtrooms can be seen. They are broadcast, but it was not the case just a little while ago. So I would like to ask -- well, later I will ask the Registry to explain to me why no images were being broadcast. That's all I have to say with regard to that matter. Now I will raise another important issue. We have quite a number of topics on our agenda. I don't know if you have the Rules before you, but I would like to draw your attention, and also the attention of Ms. Dahl, to the provisions of Rule 65 ter (H), and I will read it out slowly. 65 ter (H). I will now read it out: "The Pre-Trial Judge shall record the points of agreement and disagreement on matters of law and fact. In this connection, he or she may order the parties to file, either with the Pre-Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber, written submissions." And the points of agreement or disagreement can be explained in brief that has already been submitted, but that can always be amended since this brief is defined in 65 ter (E), (E)(i). Now, why am I telling you this Mr. Seselj and Ms. Dahl? For the following reasons, please listen carefully because I am going to go through this slowly. I have studied the indictment and the pre-trial brief and noted that, in this pre-trial brief, there are crimes that are listed according to municipalities. There are a number of crimes listed in the municipalities of Vukovar, Zvornik, and so on and so forth. And in the indictment, as well as the pre-trial brief, now, I will be very specific. For example, with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, there's Mostar, Vocin, Bosanski Samac, Nevesinje, Zvornik; then two other municipalities are mentioned: Jasko [as interpreted] and Vasinje [as interpreted]. And in those municipalities, according to the indictment, crimes were committed. And for the region of Sarajevo, there are several places within the region. I will mention a few of them: Grbavica, Ilijas, Vogosca, and others, where crimes are said to have been committed. In the Republic of Croatia there is the SAO of Slavonia, Vukovar. In the Republic of Serbia, there's Vojvodin with Hrtkovci. Hence, the Prosecution, in order to prove that these crimes were committed, will have to call witnesses and this will take time. And on the basis of my experience within this Tribunal, I believe that I am a Judge within the Tribunal who has the most experience in presiding or taking part in hearings, and I have learned from my experience that 80 per cent of the time is taken by the Prosecution and also during cross-examination to call victims and witnesses who can testify as to the crimes. The remaining 20 per cent that are crucial moments of the trial are used for witnesses relating to the direct personal responsibility of the accused. So 80 per cent crime base, 20 to 30 per cent relating to the responsibility of the accused. And, during the stage of the trial, when the accused calls his own witnesses, he will be obliged - or he's not obliged to do so, but generally the accused do so - he will cite his own witnesses, crime base witnesses, and that takes time. Therefore, if, pursuant to the Rules, an accused recognises that crimes have been committed in a certain municipality, the fact that he says, "Yes," for example, "in Vukovar, crimes were committed," that does not mean that the accused is responsible for those crimes. These are two different things. Responsibility must be proven. In our current mechanism, we will have to bring in witnesses who will testify about Vukovar. That will take time, and, in fact, that time could be used by the Prosecution and the accused to took into the issues relating to responsibility. So this is what I am submitting to you. I do not have authority in this regard; but if the Prosecutor and the accused reach an agreement, in which they agree that in such-and-such a place there were destructions and other things, that does not mean that it does not imply recognition of guilt. There are certain facts that respond to reality. Take an example. If a car is stopped for speeding, one notes that there was a crime of speeding. That's a fact. Who was driving the car, that's another issue. So, perhaps, this image can demonstrate to you that quite a bit of time can be gained if an agreement is reached between the Prosecution and the accused on factual or legal matters. And should such agreement be reached, there is no longer any reason for the Prosecutor to call witnesses to prove certain facts that are recognised by the accused. And again, "recognised" does not mean that he recognises that he is responsible for those incidents, but simply that he recognises that in such-and-such a village there was a destruction, a certain person was mistreated, which does not amount to saying that it was the fault of the accused. So I am raising this issue based on my experience, where I've noted that we spend a great deal of time calling witnesses and victims to describe to us what was inflicted on certain victims, sometimes without being able to say who did what, and so on and so forth. So, against this backdrop, the time allotted to the trial is mainly -- or could mainly be dedicated to assessing responsibility, which is really of the essence as to the merits of the case. Now, the Rules provide for this, a provision that is rarely applied. Perhaps it is not well-understood, or perhaps the Pre-Trial Judges just don't think of it or don't realise the impact it might have in terms of saving time, but I find it of great interest. Again, it will not have any real consequences with regard to responsibility, which is a totally different issue. Moreover, if Mr. Seselj feels that in the indictment there are passages relating to or there are passages relating to the municipalities and you feel it's not necessary to call witnesses because you don't challenge the fact that such-and-such a witness was arrested and detained, there, again, the Prosecutor doesn't need to call those witnesses. And, then, there's yet another problem, the fact that you have challenged the testimony of certain witnesses in your motion based on Rule 77. Perhaps, there are some witnesses that would fall within the scope of your motion; and as the Chamber had decided you will be allowed to ask them questions in this regard when they appear before us, and perhaps there will be witnesses who you will find useful and that is not a problem, but there may be others who have nothing to do with your motion, and then you could perhaps say, Well, it's not actually necessary to call those witnesses. So I would indicate to you that it is my duty to bring your attention to these issues. These are things foreseen by the Rules. Mr. Seselj, I would like to know your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree with that, Your Honour, Judge. I showed a constructiveness in 2003 with respect to that. We're now facing two problems. First of all, we're entering the proceedings in a chaotic state. The indictment was shortened last year, but the Prosecution did not reduce the number of either witnesses or exhibits. The crime base for Vocin was thrown out, the whole the western Slavonia, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, and several other places in Herzegovina, and that was thrown out of the indictment. However, on the list, we have all the witnesses that were planned to testify about the crime base in those same places, in those same locations, and all the exhibits remain as well. What does that mean then? Why was the indictment reduced and shortened? On the one hand, the Prosecution intends to prove the crime base. On the other hand, there are no specific counts about those places in the indictment. So this is the situation that hasn't been resolved, and I've been pointing to that for a -- for a long time now. And the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution has not been aligned with the indictment either. Now, why is that still the case? I appeal, Judge, that you don't allow a trial -- the trial to begin without clearly up these procedural issues. And since you have another month and a half before you or a little longer than one month, then I expect you to do that. Secondly, I was trial -- I was ready to discuss matters with the Prosecution in 2003 as offered by the main Prosecutor, by Carla Del Ponte. The only reason -- the own condition I laid down was my legal advisors be present. We could have gone through the indictment, the text of the indictment at that time, to determine what things were not challenged or what were challenge. I'm ready to do that today as well, on the condition that my legal advisors be present and one investigator per each of the crime base places; one for Vukovar, one for Vojvodina and Hrtkovci, one for Zvornik and one for Sarajevo, so the locations in Sarajevo, and one for Herzegovina and all the locations there. I am ready to have that detailed discussion to see what can be agreed and what can not be agreed, and that would save a lot of resources to the Tribunal and the OTP and would probably reduce the intensity of your intentions to bring in most of the witnesses with pre-written testimonies which enter into the documents. This is quite unlawful and will lead to an imbalance of justice in these proceedings, so I am now going to show my good well to prevent this from happening, witnesses to be brought in viva voce and my personal responsibility or lack of responsibility, without losing our way in immaterial issues. Now, if they continue to insist, then I will hear witnesses with the same intensity that testified to crime bases where I'm intimately quite conscious of the fact that a crime existed and those witnesses who falsely accuse me and where I have nothing to do with the crimes committed. So there is still goodwill on my part but under those conditions. The Prosecution in 2003, in principle, accepted this discussion but did not accept having my legal advisor present and attending those discussions. So, once again, I'd like to reiterate and offer up my offer again. We could have this discussion two or three days' time, which would save me a lot of work, and it would save the Tribunal and the Prosecution a lot of work, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now, I've listened to you with great attention, Mr. Seselj. It is true that some time ago you had already said the same thing. I don't know if Mrs. Dahl had quite understood the thrust of what you were saying. You had suggested to meet with the Prosecutor, and I note that this never took place. So what I'm going to do, I'm going to give you the floor, Mrs. Dahl, and I will also render an order, quite expeditiously, not an oral order given the importance of the issue, and I will refer in this order to Rule 65 ter (H). I will refer to the transcript and the suggestion made by Mr. Seselj and will order or invite you, urge you, to meet with the accused, who, of course, will be assisted by his advisors, in order to implement the relevant provisions of the Rules relating to admissions by the parties regarding factual and legal matters. If you could reach an agreement making it possible to avoid calling a number of witnesses, as Mr. Seselj says, but I had already said it beforehand, this would save time and resources for the Tribunal. I must say that since we've been convening Status Conferences over nine months now, Mr. Seselj has always demonstrated his willingness to cooperate, and I would like to see this same willingness on the part of the Prosecution. On this topic, which may surprise, you - myself, I did not think that Seselj would be willing to do this - so what do you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, the first response I want to make is that Mr. Seselj is simply mistaken with regard to the steps taken by the Prosecution in response to the decision under Rule 73 bis. The Prosecution, in fact, made significant reductions in both the number of exhibits and witnesses that relate to the crime bases that were removed from the indictment. Consistent with the terms of the decision, there remain evidence and witnesses we will tender to prove the pattern of conduct related to the charges, and we are also considering further reductions in the evidence related to this pattern evidence, in order to wisely and efficiently use the time that has been allocated to the Prosecution for the presentation of the case. Mr. Seselj's objection to receiving notice in the pre-trial brief of the contours of the evidence has been recently addressed by a decision from the Chamber, and I trust that that settles the matter. The point is to give him fair notice of the case, not to lard up the Prosecution's evidence with material that has been placed outside the indictment. With respect to a meeting with Mr. Seselj, as I said the last time, this was brought up at a Status Conference. We welcome that opportunity under appropriate conditions. I invited Mr. Seselj to submit a letter to me indicating what he desired. I received no further correspondence from him on that matter and considered it settled. We would be prepared, of course, to meet to see if there are areas of agreement. I would note, however, that there are several motions concerning adjudicated facts that he has opposed. Those are long lists of specific factual points that are ripe for discussion. He failed to respond to a letter putting four questions to him. As required by the pre-trial brief rules, we did include that correspondence to indicate our attempt to seek agreement. If Mr. Seselj is willing to propose what he is prepared to discuss and what he is prepared to admit and who we want -- he wants to attend with him, we will consider his request very carefully and determine what the appropriate steps are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take good note of your willingness to reach an agreement. I think it is undoubtedly necessary that you meet. It is really indispensable, which does not mean that Mr. Seselj or you will agree, but it's always a possibility. An agreement may be reached. You might as well try. It may or may not be productive, but at least everyone will have done his or her utmost. It is true that Mr. Seselj has expressed opposition to certain points; but, perhaps, if this kind of discussion had taken place viva voce, perhaps some agreement might have been reached. So I'm hopeful that a solution can be found. Now with regard to a detail, I will give the floor again to Mr. Seselj. Regarding 73 bis, Mr. Seselj, and concerning the municipalities of Brcko, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, the Chamber handed down a ruling on the 20th of September, 2007. I'm not sure that you've already received a translation in your language, but I will read to you some of the points. I don't think had you have the translation yet. It was said that the Pre-Trial Judge considers that the disposition of the decision was clearly formulated and there is nothing equivocal and resumes a decision of the Chamber, in particular paragraph 28, ordering that the Prosecution would not present any crime base motives in Bosanski Samac, in oriental Slavonia, in Eastern Slavonia. The Prosecution may put some elements which should not concern Western Slavonia for crimes in Western Slavonia, and it doesn't have a bearing on the indicted facts. This means, in fact, that the Prosecution will not call its witnesses; but if the Prosecution wants to establish the scale which is connected with the notion of joint criminal enterprise, then the Chamber, one, allows Prosecution to bring in evidence even if the municipality is not directly concerned. So that's what it meant. So the best is for you to read the decision, which will be translated for you in your own language, where all this is explained, but this particular aspect is minimal as compared to what I have said a while ago on the principle fact; that if crimes have been committed in a municipality, and that if there is who issue take been the existence of these crimes without drawing any responsibility of the accused on these matters, then there may be some facts which are admitted and recognised by both parties, then this would then avoid the bringing of witnesses on these matters. But you have to discuss these matters between yourselves. If you reach an agreement, all the better; and if you have no agreement, I will have done my utmost to find a solution. This is what I wanted to tell you. I'm therefore going to make an order, very quickly, inviting you to get together and to find common ground. Yes, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I still have not received your decision of the 20th of September, but there are some indisputable facts here, and Mrs. Dahl has not put forward the true information concerning these facts. Not a single exhibit or piece of evidence, according to the list I was given, has been removed, except for exhibits removed which were duplicates. Up to now, I have received exhibits up to number 2.500. Only duplicates have been removed, and I have found some more myself. This is the fifth time I have received Borislav Jovic's book, the fifth time. Secondly, last year, there were 105 witnesses on the list. Now there are 106. So which crime base witness has been removed from the list? Not a single one concerning these places. They are all still on the list. They will tell the story of what happened to them personally, but they never saw me in their lives, nor can they bring me into any kind of connection with what happened to them. They cannot establish any kind of link. You can do whatever you like in this respect. I have not asked the Prosecution for anything. As regards a discussion concerning agreed facts, I have expressed my goodwill, and I will not take any further steps. The initiative came from Carla Del Ponte some time ago, but at the time the conditions did not suit her, the conditions of meeting with my legal collaborators for the five locations in question. I am being tried here for crimes committed in three different states, and I have reduced this to five investigators. An additional condition I put is that everything be recorded on video camera and that the recording be handed to me at the end of the talks, and this is something that usually happens when accused are being interviewed. I am expressing my goodwill and my readiness to meet; but if this means nothing to them, then there will be no meeting. But now Ms. Dahl says that I am challenging adjudicated facts. Well, of course, I'm challenging them because they have not been adjudicate correctly. They are untrue. Even something that has been adjudicated in other cases may go challenged, both in the court and in legal theory, and in publications in general. Nobody can prevent me from doing this. But mark this: I am willing to go through the entire indictment even to correct the incorrect biographical data in the preamble. Even there, there are errors and things that are incorrect. I can tell you what they are, let alone the rest of the indictment. But I am not going to move that this be done. My investigators and legal advisors are arriving in ten days and we can have this finished by mid-October, and then you can have a clearer situation. If they want me to file a written motion, that will never happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, as I just said, I will make an order very soon on this matter. I would now like to talk about another problem with the Prosecution. I would like to discuss this matter. Following this 65 ter (H) Rule, now I'm asking the Prosecutor. Mrs. Dahl, in the indictment, the joint criminal enterprise is mentioned; and, in this joint criminal enterprise, people are mentioned who were part of this criminal enterprise: Mr. Seselj, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Karadzic, and so on and so forth. This is in the indictment. I have perused the pre-trial brief, and I have read in there that you expound the goal of the joint criminal enterprise, which was to expel the -- by all means and certain crimes this population, and you indicate in your pre-trial brief the role of Mr. Seselj in three segments: The propaganda role, the recruitment role, and so on. This pre-trial is drafted in that way. But I'm wondering, and I think my colleagues would also wonder, this joint criminal enterprise which is alleged in the indictment and which concerns persons, individuals, one of whom is present now, this enterprise, it has an origin? Did they meet? What is the connection between these people? And I don't find that in the indictment, and I don't find it in the [indiscernible]. There is a creation of an entity by individuals who have a goal, who meet, who discuss, who make plans, and who implement a strategy, after which people implement them. It seems that in the indictment and into the pre-trial brief everything which is done before does not appear. What took place before is not mentioned. One gets the impression that one takes stock of the fact that there is an enterprise and one examines what it has done, while even before reaching this stage one should wonder whether the enterprise in question exists and what are its ties between those which are mentioned in the indictment: Mr. Babic, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Seselj, Mr. Milosevic, and so on. So, Mrs. Dahl, do you think that within the framework, when you will present your witnesses, are you going to answer this question, or was this never envisaged starting from the idea that for you this enterprise is a reality and there is no reason to discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We will lead evidence to establish the entity. I would not presume it's existence. And if the Chamber is desiring a more full explication of the existence and actions -- existence of the JCE and actions of members, that can be prepared, of course; but it's fully within the evidence and the witness summaries that we've presented so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On this topic, Mr. Seselj, do you have a point of your comments to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Judge. Evidently there is a prejudice here coming in from other cases. Before, this Tribunal only Serbs have been accused of participating in a joint criminal enterprise. There are also attempts to introduce this into the indictment against Limaj and others and it has been rejected, and now there is an attempt to introduce this into the indictment against Gotovina and others. Nowhere else did it exist. I am going to challenge the very concept of a joint criminal enterprise, then I will challenge its existence on the Serb side, and, finally, I will challenge any participation by me in a joint criminal enterprise. I have never seen a shred of evidence that I participated in a joint criminal enterprise, especially with people with whom throughout the war I was in a fierce conflict: Veljko Kadijevic, Blagoje Adzic, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, to mention but a few. Another thing that's happening is the following: The structure of this so-called joint criminal enterprise changes from case to case. In my indictment, a certain number of people have been listed in the Milosevic indictment, a second set of persons in a third indictment, a third set of persons. Some names reappear, but new names also appear in one case which did not appear in another. This is also a very chaotic situation created on purpose, because joint criminal enterprise is something applied whenever there is no concrete evidence against an accused. There is no evidence that members of the Serb Radical Party committed certain crimes in certain locations, so then the Prosecution says, Well, the Serbian forces permitted these crimes; and, among them, there were members of the Serb Radical Party. So this makes me allegedly responsible for the crimes because allegedly I was in a joint criminal enterprise. This cannot hold water. The Prosecution has to establish a nexus, a link, between me and a particular crime that took place. Here, hate speech and joint criminal enterprise are being seen as a form of commission. However, this is not provided for in the Statute. By the Prosecution, these are characterised as separate crimes. Just simply participating in a JCE, according to the Prosecution, is a crime subject to sanctions, regardless of whether there is a responsibility for any of the individual crimes. In my case, a new crime has been invented, the crime of hate speech. This has never existed in international common law, and now suddenly it's a form of commission. I am using hate speech, and this is motivating other people to commit crimes. If I say some things now and this motivates someone to murder his wife, for example, oh, that's just ridiculous. That's why in a professional and legal since I find this indictment very -- it's a treat to me. Where does this crime of hate speech come from? The Prosecution relies on the precedent of the International Tribunal for Rwanda. However, those crimes took place after the events covered by my indictment, so they could cannot be used -- these precedents cannot be used in my case. In Rwanda, people have been accused and punished for genocide because they publicly called for genocide. It wasn't just hate speech, but they had "dolus specialis" proved against them, because they explicitly called for genocide. And "dolus specialis" is required is only in the case of genocide. They say that it has been proved that they premeditated genocide and had the intention to commit genocide, but "dolus specialis" cannot be ascribed to me by my means. All I can be accused of is either in committing a crime or inciting others to commit crimes. You cannot say that just because somebody listened to a speech I made on the -- on behalf of my party, in the name of my party, was motivated to commit a crime, or you cannot say that I ordered crimes. We are meeting here or coming across very interesting legal issues. The Prosecution cannot prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise because it did not exist; but even if it had existed by any chance, they cannot prove that I participated in it. However, they feel they are not duty-bound to produce evidence, to prove it. They say it existed, and we are two conclude that everything that happened, happened as part of a joint criminal enterprise. In the four hours you put at my disposal, I intend to speak for at least an hour about joint criminal enterprise, because I feel this is the most important issue. If this is not proved, nothing else will be proved. Nothing else will remain, but the Prosecution is not exerting any effort to prove this. They haven't even succeeded in convincing you that such a thing existed and that I took part in it. They cannot convince me and how can they convince the professional public? You have raised a very serious issue which should be resolved before the Status Conference, so I propose that you order the Prosecution to explain in writing their understanding of the essence of a joint criminal enterprise, its existence on the Serb example, and my possible participation in it. Some three years ago, I submitted to the Prosecution, as part of the project of my special defence, a treaties, a study on my opposition to the concept of a joint criminal enterprise. I assume this still has not been translated into English. It is about 150 pages. This study exists in the Prosecution. I don't know if you have seen it. But in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I submitted it only to them. They have received it, but they don't want to translate it. They stick labels on me. The say it is irrelevant, it's vague, and so on and so forth, but it will come back to them like a boomerang. So the same applies to hate speech. I think I have submitted three studies. These have not been translated either. All right. They will be translated very patiently here in the courtroom when I am questioning the Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, what you've just said now enables me to link with Rule 67. Now you've just said something which is quite important, and this is line 16 of page 31. You say that you sent to the Prosecution 150 pages on the joint criminal enterprise, and that the Prosecution did not have them translated. You're asking whether the Chamber was informed. No, the Chamber was not informed or served. This is a procedure between the parties. The Chamber is not involved in this procedure of Rule 67. What I can say is this: As from September 2003 to the 7th of June, 2006, you filed 15 documents under 67(A)(i). On the 7th of November, 2006, Prosecution made observations or comments, and this is somewhat the Prosecution said: "The documents 67(A) do not contain any indication concerning witnesses which the accused intends to call according to Rule 67(A)(i)(b). "Secondly, documents under 67(A) are not specific Defence notices, but they constitute quasi-judicial or factual things, and, essentially, are speeches against the Prosecution, a considerable wealth of conversations during the years." Documents 67(A) are more characteristic of a pre-trial brief which are submitted. And for all these reasons the Prosecution did not consider it necessary to have all the documents 67(A) translated and to notify the witness [as interpreted] which witnesses it intends to call to refute any specific means. On the 12th of June, 2006, you replied to this yourself, Mr. Seselj, and you said this, I summarise: It is for you to decide on the type and the specifications of your special exhibits, special defences, and the Prosecution will have to see what it intends to do. It does not intend to file specific evidence to refute the arguments of the accused. And you wrote that the fact that the Prosecution refused to have their documents translated under 67(A) blocked the special -- special defences. You asked the question how the -- how the Trial Chamber will be able to rule on your responsibility if this special defence is not translated, and you ask that either the Registry or the Prosecution would have these documents translated. This is the chronology, and I see that there is something which blocks, there is a blockage. You have indicated to the Prosecution, "Those are my defences," and so on, and the Prosecution answers by saying that it will not translate them because they do not seem in its views to correspond to special defences. Therefore the Prosecution does not tell you which witnesses it intends to refute. So that is the point we reached. All right. I could read to you Rule 67, which you know as well as I do. All I can say, and then I will now give you the floor, is that at this specific stage of the procedure the Chamber is not competent to rule on the special defences, but the Rules enables, allows the accused to let the Prosecution know what are his defences. The accused may state, say, "I haven't seen what has been translated. There is a problem." A while ago, Mr. Seselj showed there was a question of the dolus specialis concerning the joint criminal enterprise, and, therefore, he took issue with this argument. He may have wanted to know what were the witnesses you intended to call to contradict this document. Since you did not answer, he cannot do anything. So all this leads me to say that getting together, which will soon take place, will perhaps enable both parties to get rid of some ambiguities or misunderstandings. Mr. Seselj, you wanted the floor again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, should a lot of work on my part and the efforts made by my associates in preparing this report for special defence be just thrown aside with a few sentences without having read the actual text. Rule 67(A)(i)(b) is clear: "Any special defence," it says. And I am notifying the Prosecutor presenting this. A special defence is special in relation to all the other general forms of defence, and here we provide for the possibility of the existence of witnesses and addresses of witnesses, but that is not the sole evidence in these proceedings. You have material evidence, for instance. There are theoretical evidence. There is theoretical evidence, theoretical arguments in favour of something. I can bring in a thousand witnesses who are going to show that the Roman Popes Benedict XVI, John Paul II are the main culprits for the difficulties in the Balkans, and all the live authors of books that I quoted in the list that I attach. So that is the thesis of my defence. A joint criminal enterprise did exist but on the opposite side, on the side of the Vatican, on the side of America, Germany, the NATO Pact, and the European Union. That is where the joint criminal enterprise lies, with its intention to break up Yugoslavia, to cause a war, to station NATO Pact troops in the territory, to cause a civil war, and to maim Serbia. Why to maim Serbia? Because we Serbs are Russians in small. We are close to them ethnically, culturally. We are Russia's advisors. And when Russia is weak, they can destroy Serbia, because everybody knew that Russia can't stay weak forever. So that's my thesis. So they defined a Serb joint criminal enterprise in my place therein. I present a concrete thesis according to which the Pope is the leader of the Western joint criminal enterprise against the Serb people, and that he is responsible for all the crimes. And I set out my views in 4.000 pages. I written and published four books about this subject, because I do nothing without a purpose. Everything I do will be published one day. Next, there are three reports on hate speech, where I prove that the western statesmen, the statesmen of the west, the Croatian and Muslim politicians, have many worse examples of anti-Serb hatreds that they uttered in public than anything ascribed to me. So is that a form of special defence? Of course, it is. It is truly a form of special defence by concrete quotations, which I can support by documents, and I will present thousands of documents to support my thesis, if necessary. They haven't asked me to do so; but, as soon as they do, I'll supply them with those documents. Then we have a report and treatise on joint criminal enterprise, by which an analysis -- by analysing my speeches, when I sent the Serb radical volunteers to war, I drew attention to a respect for international war law, humane treatment for prisoners of war, the civilians of the opposite side. I prohibited theft. I prohibited destruction, as far as my political authority could allow me to do so. I did not have any legal authority or the authority embedded in power. So all this is contained in those treaties, and I think I have three of them there by which I prove that certain witnesses from the Prosecution; that is to say, people that are on the list of Prosecution witnesses are those whom I was sure would be brought in because they were paid witnesses in other trials, let alone the fact that they were one time spies of Serb intelligence services, spies of international intelligence services. I can prove this by bringing documents in from the Serb security service. I don't want to name any names, otherwise Mrs. Dahl is going to jump on her feet, but all this exists in all those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, as the Pre-Trial Judge, I see that there's a problem under Rule 67. You have disclosed to the Defence a number of documents. Now Mr. Seselj has described his position. I see that the Prosecution hasn't made any progress in this regard. So what I am announcing now is that I shall also issue an order inviting you within the next 30 days, so I'm giving you one month, asking you to address to the Prosecution a new version, a consolidated version of your special defence, please. And you will also submit a copy to the Trial Chamber. I would ask you to comply with the practical directive on number of pages and number of words, in order to avoid that you would be in the classical case where the Prosecution will say, No, it doesn't comply with the directive; therefore, we don't have to take it into account. So please be concise. And if there are elements that you can't fit into those 3.000 words, then put them as an annex to your notification so that the notification that you address to the Prosecution, with a copy to the Chamber, will be easily translated into English because, of course, it will be written in your language, and this document really should be concise. And I would also urge you, before submitting this document, I would invite you to read Article 31 of the Statute of the International Criminal Court. Article 31 of the Statute of the ICC foresees a number of special defence pleas, and, perhaps, your notification could draw inspiration from that Article. You could look at the grounds that are cited in that Article. This could be a way of moving forward since we are stuck right now, and we need to find ways to overcome this obstacle, either by meeting or, as I said, I will render an order requesting that within the next 30 days you file a consolidated notification. I would ask you to do this in light of Article 31 of the Statute of the ICC, because this Tribunal doesn't have any case law with regard to the special defence, please. Now, we need to take a break for 20 minutes for technical reasons,, and so we will meet again in 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall now resume, and I will raise another important topic now, Mr. Seselj, the topic of your advisors and your assistants and also the funding of your defence. As you know, a ruling was already handed down on the 30th of July, 2007, but I think there are still some residual problems to be addressed. The ruling handed down on the 30th of July, 2007 foresees two prior conditions that must be met for the decision to be implemented. First of all, the burden of proof of his indigence, his lack of means, rests with the accused; and, secondly, one or several assistants must fulfil some requirements provided for by the Rules. Now, as to proving his indigence or lack of means, Mr. Seselj, I have already said this, but I will repeat it. You need to have discussions with the Registry and provide the Registry with the necessary statements that will allow the Registry to determine whether or not you do, in fact, lack the necessary means. I am recalling this. It has already been said. Since these are contacts you must have with the Registry, I will not be involved in that. As to the qualifications of an assistant, I know recently you met with the Registry, and I'd like to reassure you with regard to some fears that you might have. The very fact that you are being granted legal aid, well, as you know, the funds -- well, I don't print the money. These are funds that come from the United Nations and are, therefore, public funds, and the way in which expenditures are made has to comply with certain administrative procedures, budgeting procedures. And in the context of such procedures, to avoid embezzlement, misappropriation of funds, graft, and so on, it is necessary for those who take part in this mechanism dealing with these funds to provide certain assurances, certain guarantees with regard to the fact that these funds will not be misappropriated to illegal ends. The assistant mentioned in the ruling, what exactly would this assistant do? Well, we could see things in the following way: You have a principal assistant, Mr. Zoran Krasic, who would help you in various briefs and motions; And, on the other hand, you have other assistants who are not your principal or main assistant but secondary assistants. I seem to understand from what you said last time that Mr. Slavko Jerkovic, is a lawyer, a member of the Bar Association of Belgrade. Jerkovic is speed J-E-R-K-O-V-I-C. So I seem to have understood that this Mr. Jerkovic is a lawyer; hence, it would be sufficient to appoint Mr. Jerkovic as an assistant, under Rule 45 of the rules, who would be the person fulfilling the requirements of Rule 45. So that's the current situation. To date, Mr. Seselj, no progress has been made in this realm, and I would like you to give me your opinion and tell me what difficulties you're encountering in this regard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, first of all, I'd like to tell you something about what you said at the end of the last session. I will accept your ruling and 3.000 words within 30 days will be the length of my consolidated special defence, but I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that neither the instructions as to the length of the submission or anything else treats this subject of special defence, and that isn't regulated by the guidelines and instructions. You know what I think of -- I think it is a recommendation, not a legally binding act. But I will abide by the 3.000 words set strictly; although, the instructions don't have anything to do with my communications with the Prosecution, and I never overstepped the scope of and range of time that the Prosecution has supplied me with documents; although, I'll try and keep to their maximum number of pages with respect to documents. Now, as regards financing, the financing of the defence, I had a meeting with Boris Petrov, the Chief of OLAD, and Boris Petrov confirmed all my fears, in actual fact. Boris Petrov, in a way, on behalf of the Registry is trying to induce discord among the members of my team, and chaos. He even tried to influence me to appeal your ruling and decision, which I refused to do, because I said I promised I would not appeal and I would stick by that. The Registry is trying to avoid payment. The question of payment is my permanent request, but it's not a condition. I'm not going to say that I won't defend myself unless you pay. I will defend myself alone and I will very literally stand alone here, because I don't intend to spend too much time or nerves on resolving this issue. My main legal advisor is Zoran Krasic; and, if my defence is, indeed, financed by the International Tribunal, it has to go by Zoran Krasic, because he alone knows what work the others did, and then we'll be able to distribute the money on a fair basis, and he worked most. And I have understood the ruse that the Registry is bent upon. They would like to have Slavko Jerkovic promoted as a co-counsel in order to be able to place him in disagreeable circumstances during the legal proceedings; that is to say, that he doesn't know whether -- what position he holds. There be no co-counsel in my trial. I am the sole Defence counsel, and I cannot risk having the Trial Chamber when it's a sensitive witness to say that we've decided that the accused cannot examine the witness but Slavko Jerkovic his co-counsel. If that happens, I will tell Slavko Jerkovic to leave the courtroom; and if that happens, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... immediately. I think there are a number of misunderstandings. Fortunately, you've mentioned this, because we can therefore overcome these misunderstandings. First of all, your assistants will not take your place during cross-examination or questions that you wish to ask. You will be the only one to do so. So I have never, even for a single second, contemplated that Mr. Slavko Jerkovic would take your place and ask questions in your stead. So you really have nothing to fear in that regard. You will be in charge of your defence. And I must say that I'm not happy at all with the fact that you were urged to appeal my ruling, and I will demand an explanation. That is not at all how things should occur. Mr. Jerkovic is one of your assistants. This team that you have depends entirely on you. You will decide who is your main assistant, who is secondary. That's up to you. No one is entitled to interfere. You are the only one to decide on the role of each assistant. This is your responsibility. The only problem at that does remain, and I would ask you to think about this carefully, is that the Registry wishes to be sure that the funds transferred will be used appropriately. Well, the Registry wants to have the name of a person who is one of your assistants in Belgrade or elsewhere who, in Belgrade or elsewhere, is an accredited lawyer. Now, why is this a requirement? As you know yourself, you are a lawyer, a professor of law, you know this is a requirement to make sure that your assistant is honourable and fulfils all necessary requirements in terms of honesty. Mr. Jerkovic, I believe, is a lawyer or has been a lawyer, so you simply need to inform the Registry of that. Well, within your team, you are the one who decides who plays what role; but, secondly, the person who fulfils the requirements of Rule 45 is Mr. Jerkovic. That's really all you need to do, and then there would be no more problem. If Mr. Krasic were a lawyer, you could say, Well, it's Mr. Krasic. Unfortunately, he does not fulfil that will requirement, so Mr. Jerkovic remains. This should not be the small grain of sand that would prevent you from being able to rely on people to assist you. You said, "If all of this is not possible, I will assure my own defence. I will defend myself alone." You've said that from the outset, and I wish you to be in charge of your defence, but I also want you to have assistants because there are so many documents, so much research to be done, and this is required by the need for a fair trial and equal arms. So what still needs to be done is to appoint Mr. Jerkovic or simply tell the Registry that Mr. Jerkovic is a lawyer. That's really all they want; and, once that is done, they will not be able to impede the payments that I have already ruled on. It would be very unfortunate if, just because of this detail, everything came to a halt, especially because your fears are not founded. I don't know what the Registry has told you, but what I'm saying is extremely important. I say this publicly. I am a Judge. I have a certain mission. And when I say to you that you will be the only one to ensure your defence and ask questions, it is not at all possible in my mind for anyone else to take your place. And to be completely frank, Mr. Seselj, other Judges shall be appointed. Once this is done, I will meet with them, and I will say to them, as I have said to you, that the Status Conferences set up a procedure that made it probable to settle a great many problems. And even though you challenge the legality of the Tribunal, you are ensuring your defence or doing your work. No insults have been exchanged. Everything has been going very smoothly. I will say to them that, if one considers appointing a standby lawyer or an amicus curiae, well, then I will withdraw from the meetings, because, in my mind, when I accepted to be the Pre-Trial Judge and agreed to provide the trial, I believe you are quite able to ensure your own defence and that there is no need to impose a lawyer, unless you were to request it, of course. So you may have certain fears, but I can reassure you that you will be in charge of your own defence. The only minor problems that still needs to be resolved is that you need to inform the Registry, unless they know it. I really don't know why they are demanding this. It's almost as if you're deliberately trying to obstruct this trial. They know that Mr. Jerkovic is a lawyer, but they want you to specify it. I think it's excessive, it's unnecessary, but why not do it? So that's what I wanted to say on that topic. Now, I also have another concern. Since we will be beginning around early November, when do you plan to have your assistants come to The Hague so that the Registry can make a plan?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I never had any intention to insult you, but I have to say, quite frankly now, when you said, and perhaps the translation wasn't correct, perhaps I misunderstood you, that lawyers can be the embodiment of honour then a smile came to my face, because that isn't the case in my country and it isn't the case in this International Tribunal. I happen to have two lawyers on my team and one who is an associate. They're not there because they're lawyers in the first place, because there are very few lawyers in this big wide world that I could trust and believe in. That's the kind of profession it is, and you could have seen at this court that they were ready for a sum of money to work to their client's detriment. Now, as I say, I have two lawyers and one trainee, not because they are lawyers, but they are experts and can help me significantly. But my principal legal advisor is Zoran Krasic, and he is the be-all and end-all of my professional team, the alpha and omega. He has to decide on all matters and his integrity cannot be infringe upon. I know of your standard principle, Mr. Antonetti, and his integrity cannot infringed upon. I know your standard principle, Mr. Antonetti, as a Judge of this Tribunal. Of course, I question and challenge the legality of this Tribunal, but I never question or challenge your honour and decency. And at a reception the Registry, Hans Holthuis or Hans Holthuis, or however his name is pronounced, said to a Serb diplomat that he was not satisfied with the way you were presiding over these proceedings. I can give you the name of that diplomat. He's from a Serbian Embassy. Then, in an Appeals Chamber decision in the Krajisnik case, it is said that apparently through your decision you solved the problem of financing. This word "apparently" was used, and I don't know if you've seen that ruling. I know that games are being played, and I'm quite sure that you will withdraw if this trial and these proceedings are not conducted in a proper manner. I'm quite sure of that. How does that help me afterwards? What good does that do me? I have gained experience here over many of years with quite a different manner of Judge, and I must have a firm position of principle if the Trial Chamber changes, the composition of the Trial Chamber changes and if you happen to leave. I have to take that possibility into account as well, because anything can happen here, especially when it's very important for this Tribunal to get through my trial posthaste, as quickly as possible. And I'll give you another piece of information. Last year, the Trial Chamber had planned out of a total of 105 witnesses to have 92 viva voce witnesses, last year, that is; whereas, this year the Prosecution, in a submission sent in the beginning of July or August this year, says that for all the witnesses it's going to ask for written statements to be included as exhibits in the list and filed. So it depends on how -- what you're going to expect. So anything can happen here, but I must prevent myself from falling into any of those traps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... on this last point, which you have expressed. There also I have to reassure you. I see that you are very worried by the filing of written statements, so I will recap. I'm obliged to recap. When there is a viva voce witness who comes, the written statement is not admitted because there will be cross-examination. I speak under the control of Mrs. Dahl who will confirm what I have you've just been saying. So there, there is no statement. Secondly, those witnesses under 92 ter Rule, such a witness, there are two different moments: First of all, the written statement which may be admitted at the end of the evidence; and, then, there is the cross-examination of the witness. So when you have a 92 ter procedure, you may cross-examine the witness, and it is possible that the Chamber may decide to admit or not to admit the written statement. Third category of written statement, the 92 bis statements. 92 bis statements is within a certain specific framework, as is said in this Rule. And in any case, 92 bis statements have to corroborate elements which have -- evidence elements which have already been collected. Therefore, there shall not be a 92 bis with a witness who would give evidence on your direct liability. This is not envisaged at all, except in the case where there would already be a viva voce witness who would come and say something about elements concerning your direct liability, then a second witness, and then a third witness would say the same things, in which case the Prosecution would request the admittance of these documents in the file. It's corroborating evidence. It's not adding to the evidence. So those statements which for you constitute a problem are those statements which exist by the situation in which the persons concerned are -- have died, are deceased. And, in that case, it is 92 quater which applies. The person is deceased. The Prosecution considers that in the interests of justice the statement has to be admitted or filed; and, in that case, a motion may be filed. Defence states its own comments. The Chamber makes a decision. But I would like you to notice paragraph (B) of 92 ter. I will read it slowly: "If the evidence goes to proof of acts and conduct of an accused as charged in the indictment, this may be an a factor against the admission of such evidence or that part of it." This means that in the case when Prosecution would only have a written statement from a deceased person who could question what the accused says, in that case the Rules indicates to the Judge that if it has to do with the acts and behaviour of the accused, the request may be rejected because this could be a reason against admitting the statement. This is, of course, following the logic of Article 92 bis. Now, I know that you have some concerns, some fears that many times you discussed this matter, and I'm trying at my own level to tell you what is the applicable law, what is the case law which applies, how the Judges appreciate and consider the application of this Rule, and how the Prosecution uses it. There are rules. The Prosecution also abides by it. Remember that I told you last time that from my own point of view we have a triangle relationship. We have the viva voce witness, high priority; secondly, a 92 ter witness; and, in the end, a 92 bis, if it is corroborating the evidence, or 92 quater in the case where it doesn't go to the acts and behaviour of the accused. Because if it has to do with the acts and behaviour of the accused, the Chamber then has to see whether it accepts wholly or partly or whether it rejects the evidence in question. Therefore, all this for the moment is quite theoretical since I endeavour very specially to take no admission document -- decision. I'm waiting for the Chamber to be constituted, or the Bench to be formulated. I will ask my colleagues before 92 bis evidence is admitted to first hear viva voce witnesses, so that we may see how things develop and not put the cart in front of the horse. First of all, viva voce witnesses; secondly, the Prosecution can file a motion or can request the admission of 92 bis corroborating what viva voce witnesses have said and who have been heard in the courtroom. That's was we stand. You have fears. I understand them. I am endeavouring to indicate to you how the Chambers function. I'm going to give you the floor, but there's just one point. On line 8 of page 47, it was not 92 ter (B), but it was 92 ter quater (B).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I am facing a real danger. You have given the Prosecution only a hundred hours for the presentation of their evidence; whereas, they have announced 105 or 106 witnesses. This rings alarm bells as far as I'm concerned, because there is an enormous danger that the vast majority of these witnesses will be presented with statements written by the Prosecution for them, admitted directly into the record, and this is contrary to both continental and Anglo-Saxon law. I have not found a single state in this entire world where such a procedure is permissible. It cannot be done in France, in Serbia, in England, or anywhere else. Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second, Mr. Seselj. You are a professor of law, and I know that you are perfectly qualified in procedural matters. You've just said something; and listening to you and looking the transcript in English, I have to correct one point. It is true that I said, last Status Conference, that the Prosecution, but I had use the conditionable tense, might have, may have a hundred hours, basing myself on the fact that the Chamber who had started the trial had decided, if I remember, 80 hours. But I have to say that it is the Chamber or Judge who will fix the date -- on the Pre-Trial Conference will fix the duration. I have taken the possibility of a hundred hours, but I don't what my colleagues will consider. Maybe they will want to shorten, or maybe they will want to add more time. I don't know. But as Pre-Trial Judge, I think a hundred hours should be a satisfactory figure for everybody. I had even requested Prosecution, and Prosecution did not answer my request. I had requested Prosecution to give me its general planification for all witnesses it intended to call. Because in my case, Mrs. Dahl, you shouldn't play cat and mouse.
